question: After their moonwalks, Apollo astronauts brought lunar dust back into their cabin on their suits. What did they say it smelled like?
source_excerpt: the astronauts also noted that it had a distinctive, pungent odor, not unlike gunpowder

extra.why_interesting: Players imagine the Moon as sterile and odourless, or guess it would smell earthy like sand. The real comparison was explosive: it smelled like the aftermath of fireworks.

topicality.rationale: A historical fact about Apollo astronauts and lunar dust, not tied to current news.

extra.verification_notes: Multiple Apollo astronauts consistently reported that fresh lunar dust smelled “like spent gunpowder” (see NASA Science). https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/10-things-dust-in-the-wind-on-mars-and-well-beyond/

explanation: Several Apollo crews, including Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, compared the smell to spent gunpowder. Scientists still debate why, because the Moon rocks brought back to Earth have no such smell.

question: The Golden Record bolted to each Voyager probe includes just one rock and roll song, by Chuck Berry. Which song is it?
source_excerpt: Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" is the only Rock 'n' Roll song on the Golden Records currently traveling into interstellar space aboard Voyagers 1 and 2.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a message for aliens to contain only classical music and nature sounds. A three-minute rock song flying out of the solar system is a delightful surprise, and most adults know a few Chuck Berry hits to guess from.

topicality.rationale: A longstanding fact about the Voyager Golden Records, not a current news event.

extra.verification_notes: NASA documents list Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" as the sole rock-and-roll track on the Voyager Golden Record.

explanation: It shares the record with Bach, Beethoven and whale song. Long after Earth is gone, it could still be the best-known guitar riff in the galaxy.

question: The Voyager probes are still sending data from beyond the edge of the solar system. Roughly how much computer memory does each one have?
source_excerpt: Voyager’s computers each have a mere 69.63 kilobytes of memory.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a spacecraft still working at the edge of interstellar space must have serious computing power. In fact it runs on less memory than a single smartphone photo uses.

topicality.rationale: A general scientific fact about the Voyager probes’ hardware, with no time-sensitive news hook.

extra.verification_notes: Correct — authoritative technical reporting and mission sources state each Voyager spacecraft has on the order of 68–70 kilobytes of onboard computer memory (i.e., "tens of kilobytes"); see IEEE Spectrum. https://spectrum.ieee.org/voyager-1

explanation: Each probe has only about 69 kilobytes, which is less than one photo on your phone. They also recorded their data on a tape recorder.

question: From about six billion kilometres away, Voyager 1 turned its camera back and photographed Earth as a speck smaller than a single pixel. What famous three-word name did Carl Sagan give that image?
source_excerpt: This iconic image of Earth, dubbed “the Pale Blue Dot,” is part of the first ever “portrait” of the solar system, taken by Voyager 1.

extra.why_interesting: Many players have heard the phrase without knowing it came from a real Voyager photo. Learning that the whole of humanity fits inside a fraction of one pixel lands with real emotional weight.

topicality.rationale: A historical space-exploration and cultural reference that is no fresher now than a year ago.

extra.verification_notes: NASA confirms Voyager 1’s Feb 14, 1990 image was dubbed “the Pale Blue Dot” (Carl Sagan’s name for the photo). https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1s-pale-blue-dot/

explanation: Earth takes up only about a tenth of a pixel in the photo. Sagan pointed out that every person who has ever lived is on that tiny speck.

question: On the Moon, an Apollo 15 astronaut held a heavy hammer in one hand and something else in the other. He let go of both, and they hit the ground at exactly the same moment. What was in his other hand?
source_excerpt: he held out a geologic hammer and a feather and dropped them at the same time.

extra.why_interesting: On Earth a hammer obviously beats any light object to the floor. Players who think about the missing air can reason that the best demonstration would use something famously slow-falling, and arrive at the answer. They are rewarded with the image of Galileo's thought experiment finally performed for real on live TV.

topicality.rationale: A historical fact about Apollo 15’s 1971 lunar demonstration, not topical news.

extra.verification_notes: NASA mission documentation and video show Apollo 15 commander David Scott simultaneously dropped a geologic hammer and a falcon feather on the lunar surface (NASA). https://science.nasa.gov/resource/the-apollo-15-hammer-feather-drop/

explanation: With no air on the Moon to slow it down, a feather falls just as fast as a hammer, proving Galileo right on live television. It was a falcon feather, a nod to the lunar module's name, Falcon.

question: There is no air on the Moon, so there is no wind. How did the Apollo astronauts get the American flag to stick out as if it were flying?
correct_answer: A horizontal rod along the top
alternative_answers: a pole along the top edge
a rod sewn into the top
source_excerpt: They designed a flagpole with a horizontal bar allowing the flag to "fly" without the benefit of wind.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has seen the 'waving' Moon flag, and many people half-remember it being used as 'proof' of a hoax. The real reason is a simple, clever bit of engineering that most people never thought about.

topicality.rationale: This is a general historical and scientific fact about Apollo-era flag design, not a current news event.

extra.verification_notes: Claim is correct: the Apollo Lunar Flag Assembly used a horizontal telescoping crossbar to hold the flag unfurled (source: https://www.apollojournals.org/alsj/alsj-usflag.html)

explanation: A crossbar along the top edge held the flag out. The 'waving' ripples were just creases from being folded up for the trip, and on Apollo 11 the bar didn't fully extend, which added even more wrinkles.
